one_liner: Rust image diff compiled to wasm32 with v128 SIMD; pixelmatch-style YIQ diff counts, about 2-6x faster than pixelmatch on large differing images.
what_it_does: @blazediff/core-wasm compares two pre-decoded RGBA8 buffers and returns how many pixels differ. It uses pixelmatch's YIQ perceptual delta with Vysniauskas anti-aliasing detection, and it can optionally write a diff image into a caller-supplied Uint8Array. The API looks like pixelmatch but is not a drop-in: you call `await initBlazediff(wasmBytesOrUrl)` once, then `await diff(a, b, width, height, output?, options?)`. The call is async, the output argument comes after width/height, and options are threshold, includeAA, diffMask and diffColorAlt. No PNG or JPEG decoder is bundled.
how_it_is_fast: It is a two-pass block algorithm. The cold pass splits the image into blocks (8 to 128 px, sized from image area) and scans them with v128 integer compares plus an integer early-reject bound: delta <= lambda_max * (dr^2+dg^2+db^2) for opaque pixels. That skips blocks with no pixel above the threshold. The hot pass runs the 4-lane f32x4 YIQ delta and the anti-aliasing check only on the changed blocks, and drops to a scalar kernel for semi-transparent lanes. The module is built with RUSTFLAGS +simd128,+bulk-memory, lto fat, codegen-units 1 and opt-level 3, and wasm-opt -O3 is applied only if it is installed.
when_to_use: Visual-regression or screenshot diffing in a browser, a Cloudflare Worker, Deno or Bun, where native addons (@blazediff/core-native) are not available and the screenshots usually differ.
Large differing pairs (1-18 MP) where pixelmatch takes 100-500 ms per call. The first-party table shows 33-73 ms on 4K and page-sized fixtures on an M1 Max under Node 22.
You need pixelmatch-compatible counts (YIQ threshold 0.1, AA pixels excluded by default) and can accept a ~0.05% difference in counts.
You want a small artifact with no postinstall step: about 32 KB of optimized wasm plus about 10 KB of JS glue, per the package README.
when_not_to_use: Most of your pairs are identical or nearly identical, as in a passing visual-regression suite. wasm-bindgen copies both inputs into linear memory on every call (about 143 MB for the 17.9 MP 4k/1 pair). On identical pairs the same repo's plain-JS @blazediff/core is 4-7x faster than this build (4k/1 identical: 2.50 ms vs 17.47 ms; same/1: 0.22 vs 1.11 ms), and on the 4K and page-sized identical pairs core-wasm's lead over pixelmatch shrinks to 2-32%.
Small images under about 0.1 MP. Absolute savings are a fraction of a millisecond, and pixelmatch/6 shows only 0.75 vs 0.67 ms.
Hosts without WebAssembly SIMD. build-wasm.sh produces only a +simd128 artifact and ships no scalar fallback.
You need bit-identical parity with pixelmatch, such as golden counts stored in tests. Counts differ slightly (4k/1: 69,932 vs 69,912), and PR #91 (2026-07-29) changed counts on images with alpha.
You need region analysis. It was moved to @blazediff/interpret-native, a Node N-API package with no wasm build.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (wasm-bindgen 0.2.100 glue is bundled); building from source needs Rust with the wasm32-unknown-unknown target, wasm-bindgen-cli 0.2.100 and optionally wasm-opt
integration.min_toolchain: Node 18+ per README (Node 20.6+ for the import.meta.resolve recipe); any browser or edge runtime with WebAssembly SIMD (v128); rustc version for builds not stated
integration.platforms: any wasm host with SIMD128: browsers, Node, Cloudflare Workers, Deno, Bun; benchmarks only on Apple M1 Max under Node 22
integration.thread_safety: not documented; one module instance per JS realm, a synchronous call under an async wrapper, no threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same algorithm family and similar options as pixelmatch, but you must call initBlazediff first, diff() returns a Promise, the argument order differs (output after width/height), and counts differ by up to ~0.05%

gotchas: Harness flaw: pixelmatch's time in the wasm table is not stable across runs. In the same tinybench process as core-wasm it ran 1.5-1.9x slower on the big differing fixtures than in the repo's separate pixelmatch run (4k/1 332.26 vs 201.60 ms, page/2 513.06 vs 267.84 ms). Across the file's own history it also moved from 287.72 ms (June 2026) to 332.26 ms (July) on 4k/1 and from 317.16 to 152.72 ms on page/1, while pixelmatch itself did not change. Against the JS-run pixelmatch numbers, the 4k/1 lead is about 6.1x, not 10x, and the geometric mean over all 34 rows is about 2.1x (derived from page data).

The headline '~51% faster' is the arithmetic mean of per-row '% time saved' (34 rows, 17 of them identical pairs), not a speed ratio. The geometric-mean speedup is about 2.3x, and about 3.0x on differing rows only (derived from page data). The package README also says 'up to ~16x faster than pixelmatch on 4K', but the largest ratio in the published table is 10.0x (4k/1).

When the result count is 0, the caller's output buffer is left untouched rather than filled with the grayscale image pixelmatch draws. Two paths do this: the cold pass finds no block above threshold, or wasm.rs's copy_output skips because DiffResult.identical is diff_count == 0, which also covers anti-aliasing-only differences. If you reuse an output buffer, check the count before you trust its contents.

Every call allocates and copies both full RGBA inputs into wasm linear memory, which never shrinks. A 4K-class pair needs about 143 MB of wasm heap, so memory-capped edge runtimes may run out on very large screenshots.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: This is the only perceptual image-diff entry in the wasm category. Pick it over WebDSP (image filters, no published numbers) when you need a pixelmatch-compatible diff count with a same-harness benchmark. Pick it over writing your own wasm kernel in the style of zaw or kmeans-wasm when you want a maintained, published npm package with the same algorithm as the repo's native and Python builds.
verified_claims_summary: benchmarks/pixel-by-pixel.md (updated 2026-07-29 with PR #91) times @blazediff/core-wasm against pixelmatch ^7.2.0 in one tinybench 5 process (25 iterations after 5 warmup, pre-decoded PNG buffers, no output buffer, threshold 0.1) on an Apple M1 Max under Node 22. Results: 4k/1 33.18 vs 332.26 ms, 4k/3 44.65 vs 423.14 ms, page/2 73.42 vs 513.06 ms, and identical 4K and page-sized pairs only 2-32% faster. The module is built with Rust +simd128, lto fat and opt-level 3; whether wasm-opt ran is not recorded.
status_note: Active (core-wasm package 6.0.1, last commit 2026-09-21, 352 stars, MIT), a single-maintainer monorepo releasing about every two weeks. The kernel and published numbers changed in July 2026 (PR #91, faster kernel plus an alpha-blend parity fix), so pin a version and re-measure on your own screenshots, ideally in your target browser.
